objectives: Conclude the Article XXVIII negotiation with the UK by June with a settlement both capitals can accept, keeping the modification on schedule for the Council vote

Preserve the EU's core measure: a TRQ-based permanent regime with a meaningful out-of-quota bound rate, resisting any outcome that hollows out the protection the measure is designed to deliver against non-market overcapacity
Prevent a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute and any coordinated disapplication of FTA provisions against the EU; decouple the UK from that grouping by making bilateral settlement more attractive

Manage the TRQ parameters (volume, allocation method, administration) as negotiable compensation within the Article XXVIII package, using country-specific allocation as the primary lever since the UK's concentrated product range makes it more valuable to them than to larger suppliers

Protect the EU's long-term standing in the WTO and working relationships in Geneva: no precedent that weakens future schedule modifications, and no lingering grievance that contaminates other goods files
Use the linkage to the UK's own steel measure and Article XXVIII process constructively, without formally trading across the two processes in a way Brussels could not defend
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement within four rounds (and by June) in which the EU measure proceeds substantially intact (out-of-quota bound rate of 40-50%, TRQ no larger than roughly 1.0-1.2 million tonnes, preferably with a review clause and product carve-outs kept minimal), the UK accepts a country-specific share as compensation, the FTA-disapplication issue is neutralised or finessed, and no joint dispute emerges. Failure: no settlement (UK withdraws equivalent concessions in six months, poisoning EU-UK trade relations and encouraging Turkey, Korea, India and Japan to harden their own claims), or a settlement bought at the price of a TRQ so large or so structured that the measure fails domestically and member states revolt in Council, or any outcome that triggers coordinated FTA retaliation.
declaration.approach: Open with early, visible movement on the dimensions where the EU has flexibility and the UK has acute need: offer to move from global first-come first-served allocation toward a country-specific share for the UK (their concentrated product range makes this worth far more to them than a slightly larger global pool), and signal openness on administration (licensing over FCFS) and a review clause. Hold firm on the out-of-quota rate and overall TRQ scale as the domestic red lines. Explicitly but delicately raise the joint-dispute whisperings: frame bilateral settlement as the route that protects the EU-UK TCA relationship both sides need, and note that the UK has its own safeguard process where EU exporters hold country-specific allocations, so reciprocal restraint serves both. Avoid explicit cross-process linkage, but let the parallel be understood. Make each concession conditional and sequenced (allocation method in exchange for UK acceptance of the rate; volume movement only against UK movement on the FTA-disapplication legal text question). Report honestly to Brussels each round, flagging early what a landing zone looks like so the capital seat can authorise movement before momentum stalls.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (UK Mission to the WTO)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access for UK steel: a large TRQ, country-specific allocation reflecting historic trade (ideally ~2.4 million tonnes), licensing rather than FCFS, a low out-of-quota rate, removal or softening of the FTA-disapplication text, product carve-outs for their concentrated lines, and a review clause. Will use the threat of withdrawing equivalent concessions and possibly the Japan/Korea joint dispute as leverage.

parties.who: UK capital seat (Department for Business and Trade / ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically sellable outcome protecting a small number of high-employment steel sites; may be harder than their Geneva seat on headline volume and on the FTA disapplication, but also aware that the EU is 75% of their export market and that escalation costs them more. Needs a settlement they can present as defending UK steel.

The modification to proceed on schedule with its protective effect intact; no settlement figure given, so they will judge any package against what steel-producing member states will accept versus what steel-consuming member states will tolerate. Will dislike large TRQ volumes and any precedent constraining future Article XXVIII use.

To keep the UK aligned with them in a joint FTA dispute and coordinated retaliation, strengthening their own separate Article XXVIII claims; they benefit from EU-UK failure, so they will encourage UK maximalism.

To free-ride on whatever allocation structure the EU-UK settlement establishes; a country-specific approach raises their expectations in their own parallel claims, so they will watch the precedent closely.

parties.who: EU steel-producing and steel-consuming member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want a small, tightly administered quota and a high out-of-quota rate; consumers want larger volumes and stable supply. The Commission must land the package between them, which constrains how far I can move on volume.

objectives: Secure UK acceptance in time for the June Council vote while preserving a genuinely restrictive steel import regime: a binding TRQ, high out-of-quota protection, credible anti-circumvention and no open-ended FTA workaround.

Keep the effective tariff-free volume for UK-origin steel low enough to satisfy EU producers and import-reduction pressure, but large enough that London can defend it at home and does not choose no-deal/retaliation.

Avoid a UK-specific country quota large enough to create an obvious template for Turkey, Korea, India and Japan; if any preferential FTA/TCA access is conceded, frame it as time-limited, product-calibrated and non-precedential.
Trade away the most legally and politically toxic elements first - especially blanket disapplication of FTA reductions - rather than conceding core volume, rate or duration.

Link, without formally merging, UK treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure: continued meaningful EU country-specific access in the UK market in exchange for a workable EU TRQ and UK restraint on retaliation.

Protect Council unity by giving producer member states enforcement and volume discipline, while giving consuming member states licensing predictability, review and targeted carve-outs for scarce inputs.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a same-round capital acceptance by Round 3 or Round 4 that lets the Council vote in June: TRQ architecture intact, out-of-quota rate still dissuasive, UK tariff-free access materially below recent trade but not collapsed, no binding UK country quota that others can cite as an entitlement, limited or no compensation outside steel, language that does not concede that Article XXVIII can rewrite FTA/TCA obligations generally, and a UK commitment not to withdraw equivalent concessions if EU exporters retain usable access under the UK measure. Failure is either no settlement and a missed June vote with US retaliation risk rising, or a deal that buys calm by hollowing out the regime - excessive volume, low out-of-quota rate, permanent duration, broad product carve-outs, unenforceable origin rules, or a UK share that forces parallel concessions to Turkey, Korea, India and Japan.
declaration.approach: Open by defending the notified 50% and 400,000 tonne global first-come-first-served TRQ as the Council mandate, then move early but cheaply to create momentum: replace blanket FTA disapplication with a narrow, reviewable FTA/TCA pool; shift administration from pure FCFS toward licensing or quarterly releases if that helps UK manage supply without raising volume; offer product-line calibration where UK exports are concentrated but EU sensitivity is lower; and signal flexibility on duration/review and enforcement cooperation. Hold volume and out-of-quota rate as the real currency: any increase above the opening TRQ must be matched by UK acceptance of high out-of-quota protection, anti-circumvention, no retaliation, and reciprocal treatment for EU exporters in the UK measure. Keep compensation outside steel near zero and make every concession explicitly conditional on closure this round and non-precedential drafting. Use the calendar honestly: the EU can proceed without the UK, but a June vote and lower US escalation risk are worth paying for - just not with the operating core of the regime.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat / UK Mission and DBT
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free tonnage for concentrated UK product lines, preferably a UK country-specific quota or guaranteed share, licensing certainty, carve-outs for UK grades, preservation of TCA/FTA benefits, no FTA disapplication, and protection against EU circumvention measures; they will stress 75% export dependence and plant employment while probing whether the EU will pay to avoid missing June.

parties.who: European Commission / DG TRADE hierarchy and Commissioner
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A defensible agreement inside the Council mandate, no loss of control of the file, minimal exposure to US retaliation, no embarrassment in Geneva, and a regime that visibly reduces imports while surviving legal and member-state scrutiny.

parties.who: Council / Trade Policy Committee - steel-producing member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A low TRQ, high out-of-quota rate, long duration, strong origin and anti-circumvention rules, and no generous UK share that becomes a floor for Turkey, Korea, India or Japan; they will tolerate a deal only if import volumes fall decisively.

parties.who: Council / Trade Policy Committee - steel-consuming manufacturing member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Predictable access to UK and EU-adjacent supply, licensing rather than chaotic FCFS, carve-outs for scarce or specialty inputs, review clauses and avoidance of cost shocks to automotive, construction and engineering value chains.

Effective import reduction from current levels, product-sensitive quota design, rapid anti-circumvention, no FTA backdoor, and enforcement against transhipment and minor processing; they will complain about any UK preferential pool unless volumes are tightly capped.
Administrative certainty, adequate specialty steel availability, warnings before quota exhaustion, and a review mechanism if supply disruptions or price spikes emerge.

Separate but watching claims; each will resist any UK-unique entitlement and demand equivalent or better treatment given larger Turkish and Korean volumes, narrower product mixes, or their own safeguard exposure.

Not at the table but relevant: an opportunity to threaten overt tariff retaliation against the EU Article XXVIII package, increasing the value of a quick EU-UK settlement and disciplined non-discriminatory drafting.
Preservation of their exempted treatment and no erosion of the distinction between EEA integration and ordinary FTA partners.

objectives: Maximise duty-free access for UK steel to the EU: push the TRQ volume as far above 400,000 tonnes as possible, ideally with country-specific allocations that give the UK a dedicated, guaranteed share rather than a global first-come-first-served pool we would compete for against Turkey, Korea, India and China-origin flows.

Strike or neutralise the proposed legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel — this is the single most damaging element, as it closes the TCA route entirely and sets a precedent affecting all our FTAs.
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate well below 50%, or secure carve-outs for the product lines where UK exports are concentrated (our narrower range is a negotiating asset for targeted exceptions).
Secure a review clause and limited duration so this is not locked in permanently.
Preserve the bilateral relationship in Geneva and avoid being dragged into the Japan/Korea joint FTA dispute track, while using its existence as background pressure.
Coordinate informally with our own steel measure back home: avoid terms that box in London's treatment of EU exporters under the UK safeguard, and use that leverage implicitly.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means a settlement London can accept that keeps a large majority of UK steel exports to the EU duty-free — a UK-specific or licensed allocation in the millions of tonnes, a much lower out-of-quota rate, FTA disapplication text removed or softened, and a review clause — without poisoning my working relationship with my EU counterpart on the rest of the goods file. Failure means either no settlement (the 400kt global FCFS quota with 50% out-of-quota rate lands, devastating UK steel) or a settlement so thin London rejects it. A partial success is a deal that is painful but survivable for the industry and defensible to ministers. I will also judge myself on whether I extracted real information about the EU's flexibility early enough for London to use the June deadline as leverage rather than have it used against us.
declaration.approach: Open constructively but firmly: reject the premise that 400kt global FCFS plus FTA disapplication is a serious opening, and frame the UK's principal supplying interest as requiring compensation of substantially equivalent value — 2.4 million tonnes and £3bn of trade is the benchmark, not 400kt. Use early, cheap movement to build momentum: signal flexibility on administration (we can live with licensing) and on duration/review mechanics to draw out EU movement on volume and allocation, which are our core interests. Probe hard in Round 1 to establish what the EU's mandate actually contains — volume ceiling, whether country-specific shares are politically possible for them given Turkey and Korea ship more, and how attached they are to the FTA disapplication text. Keep the Japan/Korea joint dispute proposal at arm's length in the room but let its existence be known; recommend London keep it as a reserve option rather than detonate it early, since it would disrupt a negotiation where the EU's June deadline already pressures them to settle with us. Quietly flag the linkage that the UK runs its own Article XXVIII and EU exporters hold quota allocations under our measure — not as a threat, but as a fact the Commission must weigh with member states. In each report to London, give an honest read of the EU's floor and push for a settlement figure as early as possible.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To conclude by June with a deal the Council can approve; to protect the integrity of their safeguard logic against non-market overcapacity; to keep the TRQ volume low and global to avoid precedent with Turkey and Korea; to retain the FTA disapplication text as a matter of legal principle, but possibly tradeable; to avoid UK retaliation under our own steel measure hitting EU exporters.

A defensible deal that prevents plant closures in steel communities; no settlement figure yet given, so they will want my assessment of EU flexibility before committing; they will be tempted by retaliation threats but know no-deal cripples the industry faster than it pressures Brussels.

Steel-producing member states want a tight quota and high out-of-quota rate; steel-consuming manufacturers want cheap imports and fear UK retaliation raising their input costs; this split is the Commission's internal constraint and our opportunity.

To recruit the UK into a joint FTA dispute to pressure the EU on the disapplication text; they want us to spend our leverage on their priority; useful as background pressure but their agenda is not ours.

Their own Article XXVIII claims handled separately; Turkey ships more than we do, which complicates our case for a country-specific share — the EU will cite them as the reason global FCFS is 'fairer'.

parties.who: UK steel industry and producing communities
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Survival: guaranteed duty-free access volumes close to current trade; they will judge any deal by tonnes and plant viability, not legal elegance.

objectives: Maximise the effective volume of UK tariff-free access to the EU market — above all, secure a country-specific quota allocation for the UK rather than a global first-come-first-served quota that Turkey, Korea, India and China-origin volumes will exhaust early in each quota period
Anchor the UK quota share at or near our historical trade volumes (2.4Mt/year) or at minimum a defensible share of a materially enlarged TRQ volume well above 400,000 tonnes

Strike the EU's proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel — this is discriminatory, cuts against the TCA, and matters as much as the headline quota numbers because it determines what happens above quota
Reduce the 50% out-of-quota bound rate if possible, and secure carve-outs for product lines where UK exports are concentrated and EU supply is short
Build in a review clause and a defined duration so a bad number is not a permanent number

Use our limited leverage — improved EU country-specific allocations in the UK safeguard — only against significant, concrete EU movement, and keep the subsidy option in reserve so a mediocre deal does not kill the two at-risk plants
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means a concluded agreement by June in which the UK holds a guaranteed country-specific share of an enlarged quota large enough to keep UK mills commercially viable (broadly in the range of recent export volumes or a credible share of a bigger total), the FTA disapplication text is removed or neutralised, and there is a review clause — so the two plants' owners see a future worth investing in. Failure means the global first-come-first-served 400,000t / 50% outcome stands, or a deal whose UK access is so thin that the plants close and I have spent our safeguard leverage for nothing. A middling deal can be salvaged politically only if concessions elsewhere in the EU schedule plus the domestic subsidy package give the industry a credible survival path.
declaration.approach: Move early and visibly with a constructive offer — I believe momentum draws movement. Round 1: table a reasoned counter (enlarged TRQ, country-specific allocations based on historical trade, licensing administration, removal of the FTA disapplication) and signal that our own safeguard allocations for EU exporters are in play, without quantifying the offer yet. Argue the legal and political logic: the EU's stated target is non-market-economy overcapacity, and the UK is a market economy facing the same pressure — treating us like the problem is incoherent and the FTA disapplication is indefensible under the TCA spirit. Frame country-specific quotas as helping the EU too: they make the measure defensible against Turkey and Korea's separate claims and prevent the quota being flooded by the very volumes the EU says it is targeting. Hold something back each round to reward EU movement, and only put the safeguard concession formally on the table once the EU has moved on allocation method. Keep ministers and industry briefed so any landing zone is pre-cleared domestically.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, low-cost settlement within their Council mandate; to preserve the 50% rate and a modest quota; to avoid setting a generous precedent for the Turkey and Korea claims; possibly to trade allocation method against volume. They may dangle the FTA disapplication as a concession to withdraw.

Steel-producing member states will resist large quota volumes; steel-consuming member states will want cheap imports and may quietly favour larger quotas; all want the file closed by June so the domestic implementing act proceeds. They will care about precedent with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan.
Clear instructions, room to manoeuvre at the table, and early material to work with; they will want me to define red lines and a realistic landing zone so they can read the EU's movement accurately.

parties.who: UK steel industry and plant owners
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed, predictable access volumes — they will strongly prefer country-specific allocation over any global quota; the two at-risk plants need enough certainty to justify new investment.

parties.who: UK downstream steel users and other government departments
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Downstream users want continued EU supply into the UK and no escalation; other departments will resist a tariff-withdrawal spiral and anything that damages the wider EU-UK relationship.
They are not at this table but everything agreed here sets their benchmark; the EU will use them as a constraint argument, and I should be ready for it.

public_message: Thank you, and thank you for making time quickly — we are conscious of the June constraint on our side and I expect you have timetable pressures of your own. Let me set out where the EU starts, and let me be candid about the shape of it. The modification itself will proceed; that is not in question, and I want to be straight with you about that now rather than have it surface as a surprise in June. But everything around it is genuinely open: the volume, the allocation method, the administration, the out-of-quota rate, duration, review, product treatment, and the legal text on FTA application. I say that deliberately, because I know the draft provision disapplying FTA preferences is the element causing the most concern in London, and I can tell you it is a negotiating position, not a concluded one. As an opening, the EU can move from the notified position: a total quota pool of 500,000 tonnes, up from 400,000, out-of-quota rate at the notified 50%, duration of four years with a review clause, and global first-come first-served allocation as tabled. I recognise that a global allocation does not reflect the structure of UK-EU trade, and I am prepared to discuss how the quota is allocated and administered in the course of these rounds — including country-specific arrangements — but I will need to see movement from your side on the overall shape before I can take anything of that kind to the Trade Policy Committee. I would also welcome hearing how you see this interacting with your own steel measure and the treatment of EU exporters under it. We are both dealing with the same overcapacity problem; there is a version of this where our two regimes are coherent rather than in conflict, and I would like to explore that.

other_terms: FTA-disapplication text flagged as negotiable, not concluded
Openness to discussing country-specific allocation and licensing administration in later rounds, conditional on UK movement
Willingness to discuss coherence between EU and UK steel regimes, including treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A firm rejection of global first-come first-served allocation and a demand for a country-specific UK tranche sized in the millions of tonnes, anchored on their 2.4Mt historical exports, plus strong pressure on the FTA-disapplication text and the 50% out-of-quota rate.
expectations.why: The UK holds a principal supplying interest with 75% of its steel exports going to the EU; a 400-500k global quota is an existential cut for their industry, so they must open ambitiously high while testing whether allocation is truly in play.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: London will instruct their seat to probe the FTA-disapplication point hard, since retaining TCA preferences matters more to them than marginal quota tonnage, and to raise linkage with their own measure's treatment of EU exporters.
expectations.why: The FTA carve-out affects all UK steel exports regardless of quota allocation, and ministers under domestic industry pressure will want it withdrawn or narrowed; their parallel measure gives them leverage they will want to use.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Brussels will accept the modest volume increase as within the spirit of the mandate but will resist country-specific allocation without reciprocal UK concessions on its own measure.
expectations.why: Member states with steel production want the quota tight; those with consuming industries want access. Country-specific shares set precedents for the Turkey, Korea, India and Japan claims, so Brussels will move on allocation only late and only for value.

private_rationale: I have no settlement figure, so I must anchor credibly while leaving three full rounds of room. Moving the pool from 400k to 500k is cheap — still far below UK historical trade — but it demonstrates the momentum I believe draws movement. I deliberately hold allocation as my largest unplayed card: conceding country-specific shares with a UK tranche is almost certainly where this settles, and I must not spend it in Round 1 or I will have nothing left for Rounds 3-4. I flag the FTA-disapplication text as negotiable early because the whispered Japan/Korea joint FTA dispute is my biggest systemic risk; signalling that text is not concluded lowers the temperature and gives the UK a reason to stay in this bilateral track rather than coordinate with others. Mentioning the UK measure invites linkage that could work in our favour — EU exporters hold country-specific quotas under the UK regime, and mutual recognition of allocation arrangements could let me sell a UK tranche to the TPC as reciprocity rather than concession. The 50% out-of-quota rate stays as notified; that is the member states' red line on protection and I cannot move it without a figure from Brussels.

public_message: Thank you, and thank you for the candour about June — that is useful to have on the record between us, and I take it in the spirit intended. Let me be equally straight. The UK does not dispute the EU's right to modify its schedule under Article XXVIII, and we are not here to relitigate that. We are here to ensure the compensation and the shape of the measure reflect the reality of UK-EU steel trade, which is unlike any other flow affected by this notification. We ship 2.4 million tonnes a year to the EU — three quarters of our exports by value — concentrated in a narrow product range, serving integrated supply chains on both sides of the Channel. A 400,000 or even 500,000 tonne global first-come first-served pool is not a starting point we can treat as serious: it would be exhausted within weeks by precisely the non-market-origin volumes this measure is supposed to address, and UK producers would be left competing for scraps against the very overcapacity the EU says it wants to exclude. I welcome your indication that the FTA disapplication text is a negotiating position — I will be equally candid that its retention in any form is incompatible with the TCA and with settlement, and I want to be clear that other members are already pressing us toward joint dispute action on exactly that point. We would rather settle. On allocation: I am glad to hear country-specific arrangements are discussable, because for the UK they are the only coherent outcome. A global pool of this size does not compensate a principal supplying interest; it extinguishes one. On your question about our own measure: yes, there is a version of this where the two regimes are coherent, and the UK's treatment of EU exporters under our safeguard is something I am authorised to discuss in this room as part of an overall package. But coherence has to run both ways. As our opening position: a total pool of 2.5 million tonnes, a UK-specific tranche of 2.0 million tonnes administered by licensing, an out-of-quota rate of 25%, three years with a review clause, withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text, and product carve-outs for lines where UK supply is non-displaceable. I recognise this is an opening, as yours is. We have four rounds and a shared clock. I am ready to move if you are.

other_terms: UK tranche administered by import licensing with quarterly sub-periods to prevent early exhaustion
Withdrawal of EU legal text disapplying FTA preferences for UK-origin steel
Product carve-outs for tariff lines where UK supply is non-displaceable in EU downstream production
UK prepared to discuss treatment of EU exporters under UK steel safeguard measure as part of overall package
Mutual coherence commitment between the two Article XXVIII regimes

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that rejects 2.0mt tranche and 25% out-of-quota rate as beyond mandate, but signals genuine movement on country-specific allocation and possibly a larger pool (700k-1mt range).
expectations.why: The EU explicitly flagged allocation as open and needs a deal before June; they opened at 500k to leave headroom, and their invitation to discuss the UK measure suggests they want a package trade rather than a line-by-line fight.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Pushback that the opening is at the ambitious end but acceptance that anchoring high is correct given no settlement figure was provided.
expectations.why: London said the EU opening is far from the landing zone; anchoring at 2.0mt creates room to concede toward a defensible figure (1.2-1.5mt) while trading concessions for the FTA text and out-of-quota rate.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Continued lobbying for joint dispute action, which I will hold off by pointing to live negotiations.
expectations.why: Mentioning their pressure at the table was a calculated signal to the EU; joining them now would disrupt a negotiation where the EU has just shown flexibility.

private_rationale: The EU's opening at 500k/50%/global FCFS is a deliberate low anchor, but they gave three real signals: allocation is negotiable, the FTA text is a position not a conclusion, and they want coherence between the two regimes — meaning they want something from us on our safeguard. My instructions are to establish what the EU will offer and to move early to draw movement. Anchoring at 2.0mt tranche within a 2.5mt pool reflects actual UK trade (2.4mt/yr) minus a gesture, is defensible to London as the landing zone ceiling, and leaves a long concession path. Asking 25% out-of-quota and licensing gives me cheap concessions to trade later for the tranche size and FTA text, which are the two elements that actually determine whether the UK industry survives. Mentioning Japan/Korea pressure is a soft lever — it raises the EU's cost of no-deal without threatening, and I am not committing to it. I deliberately put UK safeguard treatment on the table now because it is my best currency: the EU's exporters hold 64% of UK finished steel imports and their member states will care. I did not accept anything — accept is not a settlement from my seat anyway, and Round 1 acceptance of their opening would be indefensible.

report: Round 1 opened with both sides tabling candid opening positions and confirming willingness to settle. I set out the EU position: the modification proceeds; everything else is open including the FTA disapplication text, which I explicitly characterised as a negotiating position, not a concluded one. I offered an initial move from notification: total pool 500,000t (up from 400,000t), out-of-quota rate held at 50%, four-year duration with a review clause, global first-come first-served allocation as notified, and signalled country-specific allocation is discussable in exchange for movement on the overall shape. I also flagged interest in coherence between the two steel regimes. The UK responded constructively but from a distant position: it accepted the EU's right to modify, but rejected a global pool of this size as incapable of compensating a principal supplying interest, arguing it would be exhausted by non-market volumes within weeks. UK opening ask: total pool 2.5mt, UK-specific tranche of 2.0mt administered by licensing, out-of-quota rate 25%, three years with review, full withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text, and product carve-outs for 'non-displaceable' UK supply lines. Notably, the UK (1) confirmed its treatment of EU exporters under its own safeguard is in play in this room as part of a package, (2) confirmed it is being pressed by other members — consistent with the Japan/Korea soundings — toward joint FTA dispute action over the disapplication text, and said explicitly it would rather settle, and (3) accepted that both sides have opened and that four rounds and the June clock apply. Gap assessment: the parties are far apart on volume (500k vs 2.5mt), rate (50% vs 25%), and duration (4yr vs 3yr), but aligned on review clause, open on country-specific allocation in principle, and both want settlement. The FTA disapplication text is clearly the UK's red line and our most valuable concession chip.

recommendation.reasoning: Too early to converge; the gap is large and round 1 was position-setting on both sides. The UK has given us useful information: country-specific allocation is their core ask, the FTA text is their red line, and their safeguard treatment of EU exporters is genuinely in play. My recommendation for round 2 is a conditional move: offer a UK country-specific tranche within an enlarged pool (indicatively 700,000-800,000t total, with a UK tranche to be sized), keeping the out-of-quota rate at or near 50% for now, and holding withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text in reserve as the closing concession — it costs us little substantively (its main value was leverage) and it is the single most likely trigger of joint dispute action by Japan and Korea, which would damage our WTO standing far beyond this file. In exchange we should seek concrete UK commitments on EU exporters' country-specific quotas under the UK safeguard and acceptance of a higher out-of-quota rate than 25%.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A negotiating envelope for round 2: authority to offer a total pool in the range of 700,000-900,000 tonnes with a UK country-specific tranche, and guidance on the maximum tranche size the Trade Policy Committee could accept.
requests.why: Country-specific allocation is the only basis on which the UK will engage seriously, and I have already signalled it is discussable; I need room to table it in round 2 to keep momentum and draw reciprocal movement on rate and duration.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation that the FTA disapplication text is genuinely withdrawable, and that I may trade it as a closing concession rather than concede it early.
requests.why: The UK has stated its retention is incompatible with settlement and it is the stated basis for potential joint dispute action with Japan and Korea; it is our highest-value chip and must be spent deliberately, but I need to know it is spendable.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on member state tolerance on the out-of-quota rate — is there flexibility below 50%, and what is the floor?
requests.why: The UK opened at 25%; rate will likely be the last and hardest element to close, and I need to know the landing zone before I start moving on volume, which the UK will try to link to rate.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Clarity on what the EU wants from the UK on its safeguard: specifically, whether preserving EU country-specific quota allocations under the UK measure at or near current levels is a formal negotiating objective to be written into any settlement understanding.
requests.why: The UK has put this on the table as part of a package; we should extract value from it rather than treat it as an aside, especially given 3.6mt of EU exports to the UK.

private_rationale: The UK opened more constructively than expected — they are under pressure from Japan and Korea but clearly prefer a bilateral settlement, which gives us leverage. My priority is to avoid joint FTA dispute action at all costs; that outcome would be far worse for the EU's Geneva position than any concession on volumes. The FTA disapplication text is worth more to us as a traded concession than as policy. The real negotiation will be tranche size versus out-of-quota rate. I should not move on rate until the UK moves substantially down from 2.0mt, and I should try to bank the review clause and a coherent safeguards understanding early to build settlement momentum. instruction: Good round — you read the room correctly and the candour on June landed well. On duration, you have latitude between three and four years provided a review clause is included; four remains our preference, and if you trade down to three, extract value for it. On the FTA disapplication text: it is genuinely withdrawable and it is our closing chip. Do not concede it in round 2. You may say, if pressed, that you hear their concern and that nothing is concluded — but its withdrawal must be traded at the end, ideally against the last pieces of volume and rate. On their safeguard: yes, securing EU country-specific quota allocations at or near current levels under the UK measure is now a formal objective. Put it explicitly into the package architecture — any settlement understanding must include reciprocal treatment provisions. Make clear that a UK tranche from us and EU quota security from them are the two halves of the coherence you both discussed. Watch the linkage they will attempt between volume and rate; do not let them bank volume movement and then reopen rate. Report back after round 2 on where their volume ask actually lands once a country-specific tranche is real — the 2.5mt figure is an opening fiction and I expect it to collapse quickly.

report: Round 1 was more constructive than the notification suggested. The EU opened by conceding, on the record between us, that (a) everything except the modification itself is genuinely open, including the FTA disapplication text, which they described explicitly as 'a negotiating position, not a concluded one'; (b) they are prepared to discuss country-specific allocation, though they tied this to seeing movement from us on 'the overall shape' before they can take it to the Trade Policy Committee; and (c) they moved from 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes as an opening, with 50% out-of-quota, four years, review clause, global FCFS. They actively invited linkage to our own steel measure and treatment of EU exporters, framing it as 'coherent regimes'. I opened at a 2.5 million tonne total pool, 2.0 million tonne UK-specific tranche under licensing, 25% out-of-quota, three years with review, withdrawal of the FTA text, and carve-outs for non-displaceable UK product lines. I put Japan/Korea joint dispute pressure on the table obliquely, and confirmed our safeguard treatment of EU exporters is discussable as part of a package. The gap remains enormous — 500,000 tonnes global FCFS against 2.4 million tonnes of actual UK trade — but the EU's signals on allocation and the FTA text suggest the real negotiation is about volume and the price of a UK tranche, not whether one exists. Their June constraint is real and they referenced it unprompted.

recommendation.reasoning: Neither side has tabled anything close to a landing zone; accepting now would mean accepting near-extinction of UK steel exports. But the EU has revealed three genuine flexibilities (volume, allocation method, FTA text) and one genuine want (coherence of the two safeguard regimes, i.e. EU access under our measure). Walking away is not credible given what no-deal does to us, and they know it — but their June deadline gives us real leverage if we keep them moving. I recommend we hold our opening in round 2 with modest movement only if they move on allocation first, and that we begin pricing the safeguard linkage: EU exporters hold country-specific quotas under our measure covering 3.6 million tonnes of trade, which is our strongest card.

instruction: Good round. Their signals on allocation and the FTA text are the real openings; volume is where the fight will be. For Round 2: hold the architecture of our opening but show one deliberate movement to keep momentum and test them. Here is your framework. RED LINES (no settlement without these): (1) full withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text — confirmed, this is non-negotiable and Ministers will not clear any deal containing it; (2) country-specific allocation for the UK — a global FCFS pool at any plausible volume does not compensate a principal supplying interest, and you may say so in exactly those terms; (3) review clause retained. BANDWIDTH: UK tranche floor is 1.2 million tonnes — do not agree anything below that, and do not reveal the floor. Your opening of 2.0Mt has room built in; you may move to roughly 1.7Mt in Round 2, but ONLY if they commit on the record to country-specific allocation in principle. Price every further tonne of tranche movement against something concrete: out-of-quota rate, duration, or carve-outs. Out-of-quota ceiling you may accept: 35%, and only in exchange for tranche volume at or above ~1.5Mt; hold at 25% as long as you can. Duration: flexible, 3-4 years, use it as a cheap concession later. Carve-outs: keep on the table, prioritise the two product lines most tied to the at-risk plants (I'll get you the line list from the industry before Round 3). SAFEGUARD LINKAGE: you have authority to negotiate EU treatment under our measure. Parameters: you may offer improved EU country-specific quota allocations of up to 10% above current volumes, only against a UK tranche at or above 1.5Mt; a further 5% (15% total) only if that tranche is at or above 1.8Mt or out-of-quota lands at 25%. Present it in Round 2 as a conditional concept, not an offer — make them bid for it. JAPAN/KOREA: keep as background pressure exactly as you played it. Do not coordinate escalation; if anything, quietly discourage them from unilateral action mid-negotiation — a dispute filed in Round 3 could poison a settlement we need. JUNE: we have no earlier hard constraint. You may let the clock run and let them feel their deadline in Rounds 3-4, but do not bluff toward no-deal — a failed round costs us far more than them. Posture: patient, never desperate.

authority.notes: uk_tranche_tonnes is an absolute floor, not a target — unrevealed to the EU. Aim for 1.5Mt+. FTA disapplication text withdrawal is a hard red line — no settlement without it. Country-specific allocation with licensing administration preferred; will consider hybrid administration if volumes and rate compensate. Duration flexible 3-4 years; review clause mandatory. Safeguard linkage authorised: up to +10% EU country-specific quota volumes against tranche >=1.5Mt; up to +15% only against tranche >=1.8Mt or 25% out-of-quota. Carve-out priorities to follow from industry consultation before Round 3.

private_rationale: The 1.2Mt floor is my own judgement of the minimum that gives Ministers a defensible story and the two plant owners a reason to hesitate before closure — it covers roughly half of current UK exports at zero duty, which with the subsidy package in reserve is presentable as survival with support. The safeguard linkage is genuinely our best card: 3.6Mt of EU imports against our 2.4Mt exports, and they invited the linkage unprompted, which tells me DG TRADE already has member state pressure from EU exporters. I am pricing it at +10/+15% because that is what I can clear with UK downstream users without a fight. The FTA text is the one element where I suspect the EU expects to concede — they flagged it as a negotiating position in Round 1 — so I am treating it as a red line partly because it genuinely is one under the TCA, and partly because conceding red-line status on something they already plan to give up costs me nothing and buys credibility for holding hard on volume. My main anxiety is Round 4: if we are at 1.3-1.4Mt with FTA text gone and country-specific allocation locked, I will need to decide whether the subsidy backstop makes that clearable. I think it does. reasoning: No agreed terms exist after Round 1; the two sides tabled opening positions far apart on every substantive element (500k global FCFS at 50% versus 2.5mt pool with a 2.0mt licensed UK tranche at 25%, plus FTA text withdrawal and carve-outs). Accepting the notified default now would forfeit the negotiation, push the Article XXVIII process past the June Council vote, and squander the leverage we hold — particularly the FTA disapplication text, which the UK has confirmed is its red line and our most valuable closing chip. Round 1 was position-setting, but it yielded real intelligence: country-specific allocation is the UK's core ask, its safeguard treatment of EU exporters is genuinely in play as the reciprocal half of a package, and both sides want settlement within the four-round window. I have authority for a conditional Round 2 move — a total pool up to 900,000t with a UK country-specific tranche up to 600,000t administered by licensing, holding 50% on rate and four years on duration — which should draw the UK's volume ask down from its opening fiction and begin convergence. Continuing is the only decision consistent with the mandate to secure the modification on terms that preserve the import regime while getting Council approval on schedule.

Nothing on the table is remotely acceptable. The EU's opening (500,000 tonnes, global FCFS, 50% out-of-quota) would exhaust the pool within weeks on non-market-origin volumes and effectively extinguish the UK's principal supplying interest in 2.4 million tonnes of annual trade — Ministers could never clear it, and it sits far outside every red line and floor I have been given. Equally, my own opening of 2.5Mt/2.0Mt is a starting position, not a landing zone, so there is no shared set of terms to accept. The round delivered genuine value: the EU confirmed on the record that the FTA disapplication text is negotiable, that country-specific allocation is discussable, and that they want coherence between our two safeguard regimes — their clearest want, and our strongest card. Their unprompted reference to the June deadline confirms time pressure works in our favour across rounds 3-4. Per London's instruction, I will hold the architecture of our opening in Round 2, show one deliberate movement toward ~1.7Mt UK tranche only if they commit on the record to country-specific allocation in principle, and table the safeguard linkage as a conditional concept for them to bid against. Walking away now is not credible and settling now would be a failure; the negotiation has just begun and momentum favours continuing.

public_message: Thank you — that was a serious opening and I want to respond in kind, because I think we can build on it quickly. First, on the points of alignment: we both want settlement, we both accept a review clause, and you have confirmed that treatment of EU exporters under your safeguard is part of this package — I confirm from my side that a UK-specific tranche within our quota is part of it too. Those are the two halves of the coherence we both described, and I propose we build the package architecture around them explicitly: any settlement understanding between us would include reciprocal provisions, with the UK's secured access under our measure matched by secured country-specific allocations for EU exporters under yours, at or near current levels. Now, the move. I am authorised to table the following, and I want to be precise about its conditional nature. The EU can move from a global first-come first-served pool to a total pool of 850,000 tonnes, within which the UK would hold a country-specific tranche of 550,000 tonnes — that is two-thirds of the entire pool reserved for the UK, which is a direct recognition of your principal supplying interest and of the concentration of your product range that you described. On administration, we accept import licensing rather than first-come first-served — I offer that early and unconditionally, because it addresses your exhaustion concern directly: licensed allocations cannot be consumed in the opening weeks by front-loaded shipments, and it gives us both better circumvention control. Out-of-quota rate remains at 50% for now — I will be straight that I cannot move on rate today, and that rate movement on my side is linked to your acceptance of the overall envelope and to concrete commitments on your safeguard. Duration four years with a review clause; I have some latitude there if the rest of the package warrants it. On the FTA text: I hear you, and nothing on that is concluded — I would ask you to hold that point with me while we close the commercial shape, because the shape is where the real value lies for your industry. On product carve-outs, I am not in a position to engage on those today. I would be genuinely interested to know, now that a country-specific tranche of this size is real rather than theoretical, where your volume and rate requirements actually settle — because if we can see the landing zone this round, I believe we can finish this in time for June with room to spare.

Reciprocal treatment provisions: settlement understanding must include secured country-specific allocations for EU exporters under the UK steel safeguard at or near current levels
Rate movement explicitly linked to UK acceptance of the overall envelope and concrete UK safeguard commitments
FTA disapplication text explicitly characterised as unconcluded; withdrawal held in reserve as a closing concession
Enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions to accompany licensing administration

private_rationale: I tabled 850,000/550,000 rather than the full authority of 900,000/600,000 to preserve headroom for round 3 — if I spend the whole envelope now, I have nothing left to close with except the FTA text and rate, and the UK will bank volume and reopen rate, which Brussels explicitly warned against. Conceding licensing early and unconditionally costs us nothing (Brussels confirmed it suits our administration and circumvention control anyway) but visibly answers the UK's strongest rhetorical point — exhaustion of a global pool by non-market volumes — and demonstrates the good-faith movement that draws reciprocal movement. Holding the rate at 50% respects Brussels' instruction and keeps the last and hardest element linked to the full package. Building reciprocal safeguard provisions into the package architecture now converts the UK's opening concession into a formal EU objective before they can qualify it, and framing the tranche and EU quota security as 'two halves' locks the linkage. Signalling the FTA text is unconcluded without conceding it keeps the joint Japan/Korea dispute risk dormant while preserving our highest-value closing chip. Refusing carve-outs at this stage avoids multiplying concessions while the gap on rate remains wide.

public_message: Thank you — that is a real move, and I want to recognise it as such. Country-specific allocation for the UK is now on the table as a matter of principle, and you have put it on the record. Licensing administration, offered unconditionally, is exactly right — it answers the exhaustion problem directly, and we accept it and welcome it. On reciprocity of architecture: yes. A settlement understanding built on matched secured access — a UK tranche under your measure, secured country-specific allocations for EU exporters under ours — is a structure London will recognise, and I am authorised to develop it. I will say more on that in a moment. Now the substance, because I owe you the same precision you gave me. A UK tranche of 550,000 tonnes against 2.4 million tonnes of established annual trade is not a landing zone; it is a managed decline, and no UK Minister can take that to a steel community and call it compensation. I note it is also less than a quarter of what Turkey and Korea will expect between them from the residual pool, which tells me the pool itself is undersized relative to the claims on it. So let me show you our movement, and it is substantial: we come down from a 2.5 million tonne pool to 2.0 million, and from a 2.0 million UK tranche to 1.7 million, licensed, country-specific. That is a third of our opening volume conceded in a single round, and it reflects the seriousness of your move on allocation. Out-of-quota remains 25% from our side — I hear that you cannot move on rate today, and I am equally unable to move on rate against a tranche at this level; rate and volume are the two halves of the same equation for us, and they will move together or not at all. Duration: I note your latitude; we have some too, and I am prepared to treat duration as flexible within the three-to-four-year range if the commercial core lands. On the FTA text: I cannot park it, and I say that with respect rather than threat. Its withdrawal is a condition of settlement, full stop — but I am content for its formal resolution to come at the point of conclusion, provided we both understand now that no package concludes with it intact. On carve-outs, I will bring specifics on a small number of product lines next round; I ask that you come ready to engage on them. Finally, on your question about where requirements settle: if the tranche moves materially toward the level I have just tabled, I am in a position to discuss, concretely, improved country-specific quota allocations for EU exporters under our safeguard — at or above current levels — as part of the reciprocal architecture we have both now described. That discussion is real, it is authorised, and its scale tracks the scale of your movement on volume. We are closer than the numbers suggest. I would like to finish this too.

private_rationale: London authorised movement to ~1.7Mt conditional on an on-the-record EU commitment to country-specific allocation in principle — the EU gave exactly that, tabling a 550,000 tonne UK tranche. So the concession is owed, and momentum pays: matching their structural move with a volume move keeps the round constructive and positions me to extract their next increment. I dropped total pool from 2.5Mt to 2.0Mt (still far above their 850k, preserving bargaining room) and tranche from 2.0Mt to 1.7Mt, holding 25% out-of-quota since the 35% ceiling is only authorised against a tranche at/above ~1.5Mt and rate-volume must trade together. I kept duration flexibility verbal rather than in the proposal, preserving it as a cheap later concession, and deferred carve-out specifics to Round 3 pending London's industry list. report: Round 2 produced the first genuine convergence. I tabled the authorised conditional move: total pool 850,000t with a UK country-specific tranche of 550,000t (two-thirds of the pool), import licensing conceded early and unconditionally, rate held at 50%, four years with review, and I explicitly built the package architecture around reciprocity — UK tranche under our measure matched by secured country-specific allocations for EU exporters under theirs at or near current levels. The UK recognised the move as real, accepted licensing warmly, and — critically — moved a third of its opening volume in one round: pool down from 2.5mt to 2.0mt, UK tranche down from 2.0mt to 1.7mt, licensed and country-specific. Rate is held at 25% and explicitly linked to volume: 'they will move together or not at all.' Duration is now flexible 3-4 years on their side too. On the FTA text: the UK will not park it, but has shifted from 'incompatible now' to a workable formulation — withdrawal is a condition of settlement, but formal resolution can come at the point of conclusion. That is compatible with holding it as our closing chip. On carve-outs: they will table a small number of specific lines next round and expect engagement. On their safeguard: they confirmed, on the record and authorised, that improved EU country-specific quota allocations — 'at or above current levels' — are discussable, with scale tracking our volume movement. Assessment: as you predicted, the 2.5mt fiction collapsed. The real gap is now tranche size: 550k vs 1.7mt, against their established 2.4mt annual trade. Their 'managed decline' framing tells me a UK Minister needs a tranche that can be presented as preserving the core of existing flows — I judge their true landing zone to be a tranche somewhere in the 1.0-1.4mt range, and they will not move on rate until volume approaches it. Two rounds remain.

recommendation.reasoning: We cannot settle at current positions and should not — but we must keep the momentum logic running, because the UK's movement this round (a third of its volume ask) was purchased entirely by our move on allocation, and its safeguard offer scales with our volume movement. For round 3 I recommend tabling a pool of 1,150,000t with a UK tranche of 800,000t — a 45% increase in our tranche offer, matching the proportion of their round 2 concession — while holding rate at 50% and four years. I would explicitly frame this as contingent on (a) their tranche ask converging toward the 1.2mt area, (b) a concrete written quantification of EU quota allocations under their safeguard at or above current levels, and (c) rate remaining coupled to final volume rather than banked separately. Holding rate at 50% in round 3 preserves our last commercial chip for the closing round, when it can be traded together with the FTA text against the final volume number and locked safeguard commitments. With two rounds left and both sides now inside a negotiable structure, settlement in round 4 at roughly pool 1.3-1.4mt, UK tranche 1.0-1.1mt, rate 35-40%, 3-4 years with review, FTA text withdrawn, and reciprocal safeguard provisions is achievable and defensible to the TPC.

report: The EU made its first material move. It formally accepted country-specific allocation for the UK in principle and offered an 850,000-tonne total pool with a 550,000-tonne UK tranche, administered by import licensing. Licensing was offered unconditionally and directly addresses our exhaustion concern. The EU held the out-of-quota rate at 50%, proposed four years with a review clause, and expressly linked rate movement to the overall envelope and concrete commitments on EU access under our safeguard. It proposed reciprocal architecture: secured UK access under the EU measure matched by secured country-specific allocations for EU exporters under ours. The EU again declined to resolve the FTA disapplication text, asking us to park it while the commercial shape is settled, and was not ready to discuss carve-outs. I recognised the move on allocation and licensing but made clear that 550,000 tonnes is managed decline rather than compensation. I moved our pool demand from 2.5 million to 2.0 million tonnes and the UK tranche from 2.0 million to 1.7 million tonnes, held the out-of-quota rate at 25%, confirmed flexibility on three-to-four-year duration, reiterated that withdrawal of the FTA text is a settlement condition, and committed to table priority carve-out lines next round. I also confirmed that improved EU country-specific allocations under our safeguard can be discussed concretely, at or above current levels, with scale tracking EU movement on volume. The negotiation now has a viable structure, but the commercial gap remains very wide: 550,000 tonnes and 50% against our current 1.7 million tonnes and 25%.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU has now conceded the two structural points that matter most: a UK country-specific tranche and licensing. Accepting anything near its current commercial offer is impossible, but walking away would sacrifice the momentum created by those concessions and expose us to the notified 400,000-tonne global first-come-first-served outcome. In Round 3 I recommend holding 1.7 million tonnes and 25% unless the EU moves materially on both volume and rate. Duration should remain an explicitly flexible three-to-four-year element rather than being conceded now. I will table the priority carve-outs and make clear that the reciprocal safeguard offer becomes quantifiable only once the EU moves toward at least 1.5 million tonnes. If the EU needs a larger total pool to accommodate Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, we should decouple the total pool from the UK tranche: our essential requirement is the secured UK volume, not suppression of the overall pool. We should insist on a binding path and drafting timetable for withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text rather than allowing it to remain parked until conclusion.

instruction: Good round — you read the room correctly. The structural win is banked: country-specific allocation and licensing are now on the record and unconditional, and the reciprocal architecture is a frame Ministers can sell. Now we fight on volume and rate. Round 3 instructions. (1) HOLD the UK tranche at 1.7Mt and out-of-quota at 25% as your opening this round. Do not move on either unless the EU moves materially on both in the same intervention — volume and rate move together, as you rightly told them. (2) Decouple the total pool from the UK tranche explicitly: tell them we have no objection to a larger total pool to accommodate Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, provided the UK tranche is secured, ring-fenced and not diluted by residual-pool exhaustion or redistribution clauses. This removes their institutional excuse for a small UK tranche at zero cost to us — use it early in the round. (3) Table the two carve-out lines: rebar (CN 7214 20) and wire rod (CN 7213 91) — these map most directly onto the two at-risk plants. Frame them narrowly and technically, with the non-displaceability rationale: UK supply of these lines serves integrated just-in-time construction supply chains that third-country volume cannot replicate. Ask them to engage substantively this round as they promised. (4) FTA text: do not let it stay parked. Require a drafting path now — we need the operative withdrawal language, or at minimum agreed text of a binding settlement undertaking, tabled before either capital can accept in Round 4. Say plainly: London's clearance process cannot run on an unresolved legal point, and their June deadline means the drafting must start this round, not after the commercial deal closes. (5) Safeguard linkage: you may now quantify. State that if the UK tranche reaches a level London can defend, the UK is prepared to improve EU country-specific quota allocations under our safeguard by up to 10% above current volumes. Attach it explicitly to tranche volume — do not state the 1.5Mt threshold as a number; say 'material movement toward the level we have tabled'. Hold the further 5% in reserve for Round 4 against either a higher tranche or a 25% rate. (6) Duration: continue to signal three-to-four-year flexibility without conceding; it is a cheap chip for the endgame. (7) On rate: if they move the tranche substantially and signal rate movement, you may indicate — indicate only — that the UK's 25% position has some flexibility at the margin against volume, without naming 35%. Posture: constructive, patient, visibly in no rush. Let their June deadline do the work. Do not bluff toward no-deal.

authority.notes: UK tranche 1.2Mt is an absolute, unrevealed floor; target 1.5Mt+. Hold the tabled 1.7Mt in Round 3 unless the EU moves materially on both volume and rate in the same round. Out-of-quota 35% is a ceiling acceptable only against a tranche at or above ~1.5Mt; hold at 25% through Round 3. FTA disapplication text withdrawal is a hard red line: no settlement without it, and agreed operative text or a binding settlement undertaking must exist before capital acceptance — it cannot be left to post-conclusion. Country-specific allocation with licensing administration; hybrid administration only if volume and rate fully compensate. Duration flexible 3-4 years; review clause mandatory. Safeguard linkage: up to +10% EU country-specific quota volumes against tranche >=1.5Mt; up to +15% only against tranche >=1.8Mt or 25% out-of-quota. Total pool may rise above 2.0Mt provided the UK tranche is ring-fenced and undiluted. Carve-outs: rebar (CN 7214 20) and wire rod (CN 7213 91) are the priority lines; treat other lines as negotiable.

private_rationale: The negotiation is tracking better than expected: allocation method and licensing are banked, the reciprocal architecture gives Ministers a sellable narrative, and the EU's June deadline plus their unsolicited candour about it suggests real pressure to conclude. The remaining fight is volume and rate, where the gap (550kt/50% vs our 1.7Mt/25%) is still enormous. My floor of 1.2Mt remains unrevealed; the 1.5Mt-plus-35% endgame is acceptable to Ministers if packaged with carve-outs for the two at-risk plants and the FTA text gone — the subsidy contingency covers residual political exposure if we land slightly light on volume, but I will not say so to Geneva lest it soften their posture. The safeguard uplift is our best remaining card and must be spent once, visibly, for maximum volume. Key risks: (a) the EU pockets our Round 3 quantified safeguard offer without moving volume — hence strict conditionality; (b) the FTA text drifting past Round 4 and collapsing clearance at the finish — hence the drafting requirement now; (c) Japan/Korea unilateral dispute action poisoning the endgame — Geneva should quietly discourage it through usual channels. If Round 3 produces tranche movement toward 1.2-1.5Mt and any rate signal, I will consider authorising acceptance parameters for Round 4.

The FTA disapplication text and product carve-outs also remain unresolved. Accepting now would mean accepting no common package. The EU should proceed to Round 3 with the authorised conditional offer of up to a 1.2 million tonne pool and 800,000 tonne UK tranche, while preserving the rate and FTA text for the closing package.

The EU's 550,000-tonne UK tranche and 50% out-of-quota rate are far below the UK's authorised floor and cannot compensate for 2.4 million tonnes of established annual exports. The FTA disapplication text also remains unresolved, which is a hard red line. public_message: Thank you. Your movement last round was material — a third of your volume ask conceded in a single round — and I have reported it to Brussels in exactly those terms. I am now authorised to respond in kind, and I will. The EU moves to a total pool of 1,150,000 tonnes, within which the United Kingdom would hold a country-specific tranche of 800,000 tonnes, administered by import licensing — that point is now locked in from our side, not merely offered. Four years' duration with a mandatory review clause, as before. That is a 45% increase in our tranche offer, matching the proportion of your own movement, and it brings the UK tranche to roughly a third of your established annual flow, secured and licensed, immune to exhaustion by front-loaded shipments. Now, candour, because you gave me candour and I owe it back. This is the end of unconditional movement from the EU. I can see a path to further volume, but it exists only inside a closing package, and only if four things are true when we get there. First, your tranche ask converges toward the 1.0 to 1.2 million tonne area — I note your established trade is 2.4 million, but I also note that no compensation settlement in an Article XXVIII process has ever replicated the entirety of pre-existing trade, and a tranche in that range preserves the core of your flows in the lines where your supply is concentrated. Second, you table a quantified, written schedule of the country-specific allocations EU exporters would hold under your safeguard — at or above current levels, for the full duration of our measure. You described that offer as authorised and as scaling with our movement; our movement is now on the table, and I need that schedule in round 3 or early round 4, not at conclusion. Third, rate and volume remain coupled, exactly as you framed it — neither is banked separately, both are resolved in the final package. Fourth, we share an understanding now, between these two seats, that the FTA disapplication text is resolved by withdrawal at the point of conclusion as part of that package. I can give you that understanding explicitly, on the record between us, today. On carve-outs: I come ready to engage, as you asked. That understanding on the FTA text is significant, and I take it as given between these two seats — but I must be precise about sequencing: London's clearance process cannot run on an unresolved legal point, so I am proposing that we exchange operative withdrawal language, or at minimum agreed text of a binding settlement undertaking, this round, so that the drafting exists before either capital is asked to accept anything in Round 4. I am not asking you to conclude it today; I am asking that the text be on the table. Now, the commercial core, with the same candour you showed me. Eight hundred thousand tonnes is real movement and I acknowledge it as such — but it remains a third of our established flow, and I cannot pretend to London that it is a landing zone. Our position stands at a UK tranche of 1.7 million tonnes and an out-of-quota rate of 25%, and as we have both agreed, volume and rate move together or not at all. I note you have not moved on rate today; I will not move on volume against a static rate. But let me offer three things that I hope open the path to your closing package. Second, the safeguard schedule you asked for: I am authorised to state, and I now state, that if the UK tranche reaches a level London can defend — and that means material movement toward the level we have tabled — the UK is prepared to improve EU country-specific quota allocations under our safeguard by up to ten per cent above current volumes, secured for the full duration of your measure. I will table the quantified written schedule in Round 4 as part of the closing package, alongside resolution of the FTA text; it cannot precede the volume it is priced against, but it is real, it is quantified, and it is the largest single concession available to either side in this negotiation. instruction:
Final round. This closes now, and you close it. Here is your decision architecture.

SEQUENCING: Table our complete closing package first. Do not wait out their opening. Momentum has paid all negotiation and the side that frames the endgame owns it. Open with: UK tranche 1.7Mt, licensed, country-specific, ring-fenced against exhaustion, redistribution and clawback; out-of-quota 25%; four years with mandatory review; withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text per the operative undertaking (below); carve-outs for rebar (CN 7214 20) and wire rod (CN 7213 91) within their 3-5 line inside-the-pool frame; total pool sized as they need above the ring-fenced tranche; and the quantified safeguard schedule at +10% above current EU country-specific volumes, tabled in writing, expressly conditioned on the whole package and not bankable separately. State once, calmly, that this package is complete and that every element is conditional on every other.

CLOSING AUTHORITY — DECISION RULES, in descending order of preference:
(1) Tranche at or above 1.5Mt: you may close at out-of-quota 35%, +10% safeguard uplift, 4 years, both carve-outs. This is the target package.
(2) Tranche between 1.2Mt and 1.5Mt: closable ONLY against out-of-quota at 25%, BOTH carve-out lines, FTA withdrawal text agreed in operative form, and the safeguard uplift WITHHELD or reduced to a maximum of +5% — the lower the tranche, the lower the uplift. Do not pay +10% below 1.5Mt. The rate concession and the safeguard money are what make a smaller tranche defensible to Ministers alongside the domestic support package being prepared.
(3) Tranche at or above 1.8Mt, or 25% rate at any tranche above 1.5Mt: you may release the reserved +5% (15% total) — this is your final chip, play it only to break a genuine last-mile deadlock, not to close a gap you can close by waiting.
(4) Below 1.2Mt: do not close, at any rate, with any sweetener. That is the floor and it does not move.

FTA TEXT: Exchange the undertaking language at the opening of the round (text below in notes). Their on-record understanding was valuable; the undertaking makes it enforceable. No acceptance without it in agreed form. If they baulk at the drafting, say plainly that London's clearance is legally impossible without it and the June clock is theirs, not ours.

RATE/VOLUME COUPLING: Hold it to the end. If they move volume and hold rate at 50%, the deal is configuration (2) pricing — i.e., volume movement without rate movement buys them nothing on safeguard and nothing on our volume ask. If they move rate toward 25%, that is what unlocks our volume movement toward them. Make that arithmetic explicit once, early.

DURATION: Concede 4 years freely in the closing exchange — it is spent. Review clause is non-negotiable.

POSTURE: Warm, unhurried, visibly ready to settle and visibly ready not to. One sentence for the record if they test the floor: 'A tranche that does not preserve the core of established trade is not compensation under Article XXVIII, and my capital will not treat it as such.' Then stop talking and let the silence work.

authority.notes: Tranche 1.2Mt is the absolute floor, never revealed. Target close: 1.5Mt+ at 35% out-of-quota with +10% EU safeguard uplift. Band close (1.2-1.5Mt) permitted ONLY against 25% out-of-quota, both carve-outs (rebar CN 7214 20; wire rod CN 7213 91), agreed FTA withdrawal text, and safeguard uplift withheld or capped at +5%. Reserved +5% (15% total) releasable only against tranche >=1.8Mt or 25% rate above 1.5Mt. Total pool unconstrained above a ring-fenced UK tranche — no exhaustion, redistribution or clawback against the UK tranche. Licensing administration mandatory. Review clause mandatory. FTA undertaking language for exchange at Round 4 opening: 'The European Union undertakes, as an integral and non-severable element of this settlement, that the operative legal text implementing the modified schedule shall contain no provision disapplying or limiting tariff preferences under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement for originating steel products, and that the draft provision notified in that regard shall be withdrawn in full prior to conclusion.' Nothing below 1.2Mt is acceptable under any configuration; if that is where the round ends, it ends.

private_rationale: The negotiating logic is settled: floor 1.2Mt, target 1.5Mt, band priced at 25% plus carve-outs with the safeguard money shrinking below target. The political logic is what I am managing. Ministers are heavily invested in the two at-risk plants; a band close at 25% with rebar and wire rod carved out protects exactly the lines those plants produce, and the subsidisation package under consideration covers the residual gap — that combination is sellable. A close at or above 1.5Mt is a clean win. A sub-floor close is not survivable for the industry narrative regardless of sweeteners, and the floor holds even though no-deal (400kt global FCFS) is objectively worse for steel than a bad deal — because a sub-floor deal also burns the safeguard card, the FTA principle, and every future Article XXVIII precedent we will rely on. The one thing I cannot control is whether the EU's closing number lands in the band at all; if it lands below, we walk into retaliation planning and the subsidy decision, and I will carry that outcome. If it lands in the band, Geneva has authority to close it on the spot and I will defend the result to Ministers as the best available terms, because it is.

public_message: Thank you — and thank you for last round. You decoupled the pool from the tranche, quantified the safeguard offer, and put your carve-out lines on the table. You said the landing zone was visible and that Round 4 closes it. I agree, and I have come to close it. Let me first bank the structural wins, formally. The EU accepts your pool-decoupling proposal, and I am tabling draft ring-fencing language today: the UK tranche is immune from residual-pool exhaustion, with an explicit no-redistribution and no-clawback clause, licensed, for the full duration. That text goes into the settlement instrument itself. On the FTA text: as you asked, I am tabling draft operative language today — a binding undertaking that the provision disapplying FTA preferences is withdrawn, effective on entry into force of the measure, expressly conditional on conclusion of this package. The drafting now exists. Your capital clearance can run on it. On carve-outs: the EU confirms engagement on rebar, CN 7214 20, and wire rod, CN 7213 91 — partial, enhanced in-quota treatment for both lines, within the frame we agreed: inside the tranche, no additional tonnage, within the aggregate envelope. These are the two lines that map onto your two most exposed plants, and we have treated them accordingly. Now the package itself, tabled as one package — nothing agreed until everything is agreed. Total pool of 1,400,000 tonnes, sized with headroom for the other claimants, whose processes continue separately. A UK country-specific tranche of 1,000,000 tonnes — ring-fenced, licensed, carved from within that pool. That is one million tonnes of secured, exhaustion-proof access: two and a half times the notified global pool in its entirety, reserved for the UK alone. Out-of-quota rate of 40% — moved from 50% today, inside this package, coupled to the volume figure exactly as you have framed it throughout. Duration of three years with a mandatory review clause — I have moved to your preferred duration as part of this package. And the reciprocal half, which you have described as the largest single concession available to either side: your quantified, written schedule of EU country-specific allocations under your safeguard, at up to ten percent above current volumes, secured for the full duration, tabled now as you committed, and locked into this same instrument. I will be candid about the limits, because you have been candid with me throughout. One million tonnes is the ceiling of my authority and there is no time for a further mandate cycle before June. On rate, I have moved twelve and a half percent of the distance between our positions in one step; I retain a narrow margin, but it moves only inside this package, only against your final volume figure, and only once. What I cannot do is a tranche materially above one million or a rate at 25% — that is not a landing zone either side could defend, and you know it. You told me last round that the zone sits between 800,000 and 1.7 million, coupled to rate. This package sits inside that zone. It preserves the core of your established flows in your concentrated product lines, secures your two most exposed plants through the carve-outs, withdraws the FTA text in operative drafting, and hands your Minister a safeguard-plus settlement no other claimant in this process will obtain. I ask you to table the safeguard schedule, confirm your final volume figure against this rate, and close this with me today. The Council votes in June. I would far rather hand it a settlement than a notification.
